title: Periodic Table Adventure 2 · Calculations
welcome_lead: Time to explain the trends — why group 1 gets more reactive down the group and why group 7 gets less.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry Periodic Table trends — reactivity of group 1 and group 7, atomic radius, electron configurations of the first 20 elements.
final_note: You can explain group 1 and group 7 reactivity trends using shells and atomic radius, and write configurations for the first 20 elements.

concepts.def: Size of an atom; grows down a group.
Inner shells block the nucleus pulling outer electrons.
Reactivity increases down group 1 (Li to Cs).
Reactivity decreases down group 7 (F to I).
G1 wants to lose 1; easier when atom is bigger.
G7 wants to gain 1; harder when atom is bigger.

walkthroughs.body_html:
As you go down a group, atoms get bigger and the outer shell is further from the nucleus.

Extra inner shells also shield the outer electron from the positive nucleus. So the outer electron is held less tightly.

Group 1 metals react by losing their one outer electron. Bigger atom + more shielding = easier to lose.

So reactivity goes up from lithium to caesium. Potassium reacts with water more fiercely than sodium, which is more fierce than lithium.

Halogens react by gaining one electron. A bigger atom means the new electron lands further out, where the pull is weaker.

So reactivity goes down from fluorine to iodine. Fluorine is the most reactive; iodine the least. For the first 20 elements you fill shells 2, 8, 8, 2.

mcqs.q: Which group 1 metal is the MOST reactive of these?
Why does reactivity decrease down group 7?
options: The outer shell is closer to the nucleus
Bigger atoms attract a new electron less strongly

numericals.q: Calcium has atomic number 20. How many electrons are in its outer shell?

free_texts.q: Write the electron configuration of magnesium (Z = 12). Use the form 2,8,1 — no spaces.
free_texts.hint: Fill 2, then 8, then put the rest in shell 3.
